newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria's Vranitzky calls for swift CA decision.
newsitem.headline: Austria's Vranitzky calls for swift CA decision.

text.p: Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky said on Wednesday a decision on the sale of privatisation candidate Creditanstalt had to follow a January 10 deadline swiftly.

"A decision must swiftly be made after the 10th for the best bidder and the highest offer. We're committed to that," Vranitzky told a news conference opening the Social Democratic Party's annual convention in this southern Austrian spa town.

Vranitzky declined to be drawn on a specific date for the sale decision, but added: "If we let it drag on it would hardly conjure up a good impression of the decision-making capacity of the government."
The privatisation of Creditanstalt was first planned in 1991 and has become Europe's longest running sell-off saga.
Finance Minister Viktor Klima has given three existing bidders for the state's 70 percent stake in Creditanstalt, the country's second-biggest bank, a final deadline of Friday to improve their bids.
The Social Democrat's junior coalition partner, the conservative People's Party, has called for a special session of parliament on January 14 to discuss the contested sale.

The conservatives want the bank to be sold to a group of bidders led by EA-Generali. But the dominant Social Democrats strongly prefer a sale to market leader Bank Austria, which has topped EA-Generali's bid by almost three billion schillings ($272.3 million).

Vranitzky stressed it was solely up to the finance minister to choose the winner. "I stress again it is Klima's decision and it is independent from the special parliamentary session. We are not going to be bullied into a decision," he said.

The chancellor flatly rejected a compromise solution offered by the People's Party on Tuesday, according to which half the state's stake in Creditanstalt should be sold to Bank Austria and the rest be floated on the stock exchange.
"This is a bad option...the law dictates that we sell to the highest bidder," Vranitzky said.
The increasingly heated debate over the sale of Creditanstalt has driven a wedge between the two government partners, threatening a collapse of their uneasy one-year old coalition.
